item.title: Everything you've got wrong about daylight saving time
item.description:
With clocks falling back this weekend, The Pour Over takes on the myths around daylight saving time — what it actually does, why it exists, and what people commonly get wrong about it. The piece untangles the history and the health and safety debates that resurface every spring and fall.

It's a timely explainer for the annual ritual: less about the one-hour shift itself, and more about why the argument over permanent daylight saving (or permanent standard time) never seems to settle.

item.title: One Week to the Midterms: Obama and Trump Hit the Trail, Alaska Lawsuit Roils a Senate Race
item.description:
With the midterms just over a week away, the campaign trail crowded further this weekend. Former President Obama stumped for Democrats in Ohio and Michigan, calling the elections Democrats' "last best chance" to curb President Trump's "chaos and cruelty," while Trump toured battleground states to boost vulnerable Republicans, announcing a $4.2 billion Audi plant in Georgia and an executive order ending 50% tariffs on Canadian agricultural imports that had squeezed businesses in states like Maine.

Meanwhile, Alaska's high-stakes Senate race took a strange turn: the Justice Department sued to block certification if Democrat Mary Peltola wins, arguing a candidate sharing the name of Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan ran "with the intention of misleading" his supporters. The case adds a legal wrinkle to an already tight race days before voters decide.

Sources

  • The Pour Over: New York's Neigh

item.title: Protests Flare Across Europe as France Enters a Fifth Week of Unrest
item.description:
Demonstrations swept Europe over the weekend as protests over living costs, corruption, and wars in the Middle East flared in Italy, Spain, Portugal, and Albania. Italy deployed soldiers to Rome, Milan, and other cities to quell riots, and several hundred protesters stormed the Roman Colosseum on Saturday. France, meanwhile, entered its fifth week of mass protests, with at least 410,000 people gathering nationwide; tighter security and curfews kept violence somewhat lower than the prior weekend, with about 1,300 arrests, down from roughly 2,600.

Amid the unrest, the NFL still played its first-ever game in Paris, a Steelers-Saints matchup, though some outside-the-stadium events were closed over accessibility concerns. The juxtaposition captures a continent where daily life and spectacle are proceeding against a backdrop of deep discontent.

Sources

  • The Pour Over: New York's Neigh

item.title: New York City Says Neigh to Horse-Drawn Carriages
item.description:
New York City is ending its 170-year-old horse-drawn carriage industry. The City Council voted 40-7 on Thursday to ban the tourist carriages by 2028, following the June death of an 18-year-old who jumped from a runaway carriage. Supporters of the ban called the industry a serious safety risk, while critics, including President Trump, defended the carriages as a quintessential New York experience.

The vote closes a long-running debate between animal-welfare and safety advocates on one side and carriage drivers and tourism interests on the other. With the ban set for 2028, the industry has a runway to wind down, but the Central Park carriage rides that defined the experience for generations are now on a countdown.

item.title: Brewers Lead the World Series 2-0; Valkyries Even the WNBA Finals
item.description:
It's crunch time for baseball and basketball. The Milwaukee Brewers took a 2-0 World Series lead over the Tampa Bay Rays on Saturday with their seventh postseason comeback win, while the Golden State Valkyries evened the WNBA Finals 2-2 by slowing Atlanta Dream star Angel Reese, whose double-doubles in the first three games had been a nightmare for Golden State. Both series resume tonight.

Off the field, a different drama looms: an MLB lockout looks likely to begin December 1 when the current labor agreement expires. Owners want a salary cap to curb spending gaps and improve competitive balance, while the players' union vows never to accept one, pointing to this Fall Classic, the first since 1991 between two bottom-half spenders, as proof nothing is broken. The 2027 season could be at risk.

Sources

  • The Pour Over: New York's Neigh
